title: Prescription problems; Fatality inquiry hears of Colleen Akazay's medication woes
article: Much of the second day of the inquiry into the death of Colleen Marie Akazay focused on the medication she had been prescribed in the months before her death, and her behaviour just hours before she was found unresponsive in an RCMP holding cell last year.
Dr. Andries Botha was on the witness stand for nearly three hours on Friday and recounted much of Akazay's medical and prescription history from 1997 until her death on Feb. 18, 2006.

The picture painted was that of a woman with a wide variety of health issues - ranging from chronic back aches to depression as well as anxiety and stress disorders - all of which Botha treated with medication.

Court heard on Friday morning that, though Botha had warned Akazay on numerous occasions not to exceed the maximum dosage of the Tylenol 4 and bromazepam, he and other doctors often prescribed her pills far in excess of what would be considered an average therapeutic dosage.
Botha explained that, on one or two occasions Akazay came to him claiming she had either lost or had been robbed of her medication, which prompted him to write her new prescriptions.
The vast majority of prescriptions he and other doctors wrote for two or three times the average therapeutic use were unexplained.

Medical and prescription records also showed Akazay had been "triple-doctoring," or seeing three doctors for prescriptions. Botha said he was unaware of most, if not all, of those visits to other doctors.

Records read out in court showed that, less than 72 hours before her death, Botha prescribed Akazay 100 tablets of Tylenol 4. He explained he was going away for an extended period of time and hoped to supply Akazay with enough medication to last her until she could make an appointment with another doctor.
However, records showed that that prescription was filled as an order for 120 pills at the Grimshaw Value Drug Mart.
That prescription was one of many which landed Akazay often two or three times the prescribed amount of medication. They were all filled at the same pharmacy.
This discrepancy between what was prescribed and what was dispensed was not explained in court.

Botha said he was unaware of this happening, as he was unaware that, in addition to her prescribed medication, Akazay was also buying non-prescription extra-strength Tylenol and Tylenol 1 pills by the hundreds.
Had he known, he said in court, he would have reconsidered the amount of medication he prescribed her.
More light was also shed on the last few hours of Akazay's life when RCMP Const. Helen Pappas took the stand Friday.
Pappas was one of three officers who arrested Akazay and her common-law husband and took them down to the RCMP cells.

In stark contrast with testimony heard on Thursday - where Akazay's temporary cellmate said Akazay was having trouble with simple tasks such as staying awake, going to the bathroom and getting into bed - Pappas said Akazay was alert and coherent.
"We were talking, we were on good terms ... this was a shock to me when I heard (that she died) in the morning," said Pappas.

"At this point I thought she was fit (for incarceration). There was nothing to indicate that she was in any medical duress," she added, pointing out that when she asked Akazay why she dozed off at one point, Akazay told her that it was because she had been awake for 24 hours.

Many questions addressed to Pappas revolved around her medical training - basic first aid, CPR and artificial respiration, she told court - and the lack of a medical professional on duty at the detachment.
Pappas was then asked if she would take additional medical training if it was available. She answered with a confident: "To prevent this? Absolutely."
There were also some questions arising from her testimony being at odds with the sheet that was filled out upon Akazay's booking into cells.
Marked on that sheet were "falling" for balance and "incoherent" in the section for speech.
Pappas disagreed with those findings and said she was not the officer who wrote those observations.

Though the inquiry was originally scheduled for Thursday and Friday, there are a number of police and civilian witnesses who had not yet taken the stand to testify before Grande Prairie provincial court Judge Jim Watson.
They are expected to testify sometime early next year.
A specific date for the fatality to resume has not yet been scheduled.
Public inquiries held under the Fatality Inquiries Act are limited to establishing the cause, manner, time, place and circumstances of death, as well as the identity of the deceased.
The judge may make recommendations on the prevention of similar occurrences but is prohibited, under the act, from making findings of legal responsibility or assigning blame.
Fatality inquiries are scheduled after all investigations have been completed.
